questions_asked: On these Seattle highways at rush hour, do cars mostly stay in the right lane with the left lanes free, or does every lane end up packed?
On a busy Seattle freeway, about what fraction of the day's total cars pass during the morning rush hour?
Roughly how many cars can a single busy freeway lane carry per hour before it starts backing up?
Compared with a human driver, can a coordinated self-driving car follow another car at roughly half the usual gap distance?
When a self-driving car follows a human driver in traffic, does it still gain from driving closer than usual?
If one freeway lane were reserved for self-driving cars, would human drivers still speed into the open lanes?
In a traffic jam, can self-driving cars safely drive faster than the human traffic around them?
If only a few percent of cars were self-driving, would those cars really form long smooth driving groups?
When a freeway runs at full capacity, does traffic eventually settle into a steady slow flow, or does it keep surging?
Roughly what share of self-driving cars would drivers need before the stop-and-go traffic clearly eased?
expert_answers: Every lane ends up packed. At rush hour on I-5, I-90, I-405, and SR-520, demand exceeds capacity, so traffic fills all available lanes roughly uniformly; the left lanes are not left free. Lane-use differences (right lanes heavier from merging/exiting, left lanes used by through traffic) exist but do not leave lanes empty. This is the defining feature of congested flow: density is high across the full cross-section, which is why adding self-driving cars to raise effective capacity is the premise of the problem.

Morning rush hour (roughly 6–9 a.m.) typically carries on the order of 20–30% of a freeway's daily traffic on these Seattle corridors. A commonly used planning figure is that the peak hour alone is about 8–10% of daily traffic, and the 3-hour morning peak is roughly 20–25% of the daily total. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise measured value.

About 1,800–2,000 cars per hour per lane is the standard planning capacity for a freeway lane; beyond roughly 2,000 vehicles/hour/lane, flow becomes unstable and queues form. In practice, congestion on these Seattle corridors begins to set in around 1,500–1,800 veh/h/lane, and throughput can actually drop once breakdown occurs. These are standard empirical figures, not precise measured values.

Yes — roughly. A coordinated self-driving car with vehicle-to-vehicle communication and fast, precise actuation can follow at about half the normal gap, because its reaction time is far shorter than a human's (tens of milliseconds vs. ~1–1.5 s) and it can brake and accelerate smoothly and predictably.

The practical limit is not reaction time but physics and safety: at highway speed, half the usual gap still leaves a stopping-distance margin that must cover braking capability, sensor/actuation latency, and the lead vehicle's own braking. So halving the gap is realistic at moderate speeds and in coordinated platoons, but the achievable reduction shrinks at high speed and in mixed traffic where the lead car is human-driven and unpredictable. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

Yes, but only partially. A self-driving car following a human-driven lead still gains from a shorter gap, because its own reaction time is far shorter than a human's, so it can safely run a smaller headway than a human follower would. The gain is smaller than in a self-driving-follows-self-driving platoon: the lead human's unpredictable braking forces the follower to keep a larger safety margin, so the achievable gap reduction is maybe a third to a half rather than the full halving seen in coordinated platoons. The benefit also shrinks at high speed, where stopping distance dominates. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

Yes. If a lane is reserved for self-driving cars, human drivers will still enter it — especially when the general lanes are congested and the reserved lane is visibly moving faster. This is the standard "empty lane" violation problem: compliance is imperfect, enforcement is difficult and costly, and the incentive to cheat rises exactly when congestion is worst. So a dedicated lane cannot be modeled as perfectly exclusive; expect a nonzero fraction of human vehicles using it, which erodes the capacity benefit and can create a mixed-flow lane rather than a clean separation. This is an empirical judgment about driver behavior, not a precise figure.

No — not safely, and not in a way that helps. In a jam, a self-driving car is constrained by the vehicle immediately ahead, which is human-driven and unpredictable. It cannot pass through or over that car, and it cannot safely exceed the speed of the car it is following; doing so would eliminate its safety margin and risk rear-ending the lead vehicle. Its advantage is shorter reaction time and smoother braking, which lets it follow at a smaller gap and damp stop-and-go waves, not drive faster than the surrounding traffic. Any speed above the local flow would require a clear lane, which in a jam does not exist.

No. At a few percent penetration, self-driving cars are sparse and randomly scattered through the traffic stream, so they rarely encounter each other. Platooning requires consecutive self-driving vehicles in the same lane, and at low penetration the probability of that is very small — most self-driving cars are isolated and must follow human-driven vehicles, gaining only the partial headway benefit. Long smooth groups only begin to form at much higher penetration (roughly tens of percent), and become common only when self-driving cars are a large share of the flow. This is an empirical judgment about platoon formation, not a precise figure.

It keeps surging. At full capacity, freeway flow is unstable rather than settling into a steady slow state: small disturbances (a driver braking, a merge, a lane change) amplify into stop-and-go waves that propagate backward through the queue. Traffic oscillates between brief accelerations and braking, so speeds and flows surge and collapse repeatedly rather than holding a constant low value. A genuinely steady slow flow can occur in some congested regimes, but at capacity the characteristic behavior is oscillation — this is the well-documented "breakdown" and stop-and-go instability of congested freeways. This is an empirical characterization, not a precise figure.

Roughly 30–50% penetration before stop-and-go clearly eases, with the marked improvement typically appearing in the upper part of that range (around 40–50%). Below about 20–30%, self-driving cars are too sparse to form enough consecutive platoons, so they only damp waves locally and the jam persists. The easing comes from a large enough share of vehicles following at short, smooth headways to absorb disturbances before they amplify. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.
